SS0101.name: Juba
SS0101.livelihoods: Mostly crop farming, mainly sorghum, with a few livestock. There is one rainy season and not enough cereal, so people turn to forest and wild foods and sell bush products.
SS0101.history: Juba County holds Juba, the national capital and county seat. It is multi-ethnic: the host communities include the Bari, Lokoya and Lulubo, and its payams include Rejaf, Gondokoro, Mangalla, Lobonok and Wonduruba.
SS0101.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported fighting between the national army (SSPDF) and the National Salvation Front (NAS) that harmed civilians in Juba County in 2023 and 2024, and armed incursions by Murle groups near Gondokoro and Mangalla in 2023. ACLED has recorded more political-violence events in Juba than in any other county since 2018. Deaths are among the highest in the country and peaked in 2023, and civilians are often the target. The displaced population is one of the largest in South Sudan and peaked in 2024. Communal clashes and floods have each displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and since 2023 many people fleeing the war in Sudan have come to Juba. Hunger is less widespread than in most counties, but about half of residents were still in crisis-level hunger or worse in 2024 and 2025.

SS0102.name: Kajo-keji
SS0102.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS0102.history: Home mainly to the Kuku, on the border with Uganda. It was once seen as a stable model county, but conflict emptied much of it from 2016.
SS0102.conflict_impact: UNMISS found Kajo-Keji and Yei among the areas worst hit by fighting between government forces and the National Salvation Front (NAS) in 2018-19, and the two sides clashed in parts of the county again in 2024. By ACLED's count, political violence here is moderate compared with other counties, and 2025 was the deadliest year. Displacement peaked in 2018, during that conflict, and communal violence has since displaced tens of thousands more. In 2018 more than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger or worse. Things have eased somewhat, but a large minority are still in serious need.

SS0103.name: Lainya
SS0103.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS0103.history: Lainya lies on the Juba-Yei road, with its headquarters at Lainya town, and was part of the former Yei River State. The National Salvation Front (NAS) insurgency has affected it since 2016-17.
SS0103.conflict_impact: Villages in Lainya and neighbouring Yei, Mukaya among them, were attacked again and again in 2018-19. UNMISS blamed the National Salvation Front (NAS) for many of the abductions in Mukaya payam in 2022. ACLED records a relatively high level of political violence for the county, with the most deaths in 2019. The displaced population was fairly large and peaked in 2021, and communal clashes have driven thousands more from their homes. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger or worse in 2018. That share has fallen, but it is still substantial.

SS0104.name: Morobo
SS0104.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS0104.history: A Greenbelt county on the borders of Uganda and DR Congo. Most residents are Kakwa, Keliko and Lugbara farmers, and the county supplies food to Yei and Juba.
SS0104.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented abductions by the National Salvation Front (NAS) in Morobo in 2022-23. In 2025 the national army (SSPDF) bombed SPLA-IO positions from the air, including the Kendila cantonment site. Political violence is moderate in ACLED's data, and deaths were highest in 2025. Displacement peaked in 2022, and fighting between armed forces has forced thousands from their homes since 2020. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0105.name: Terekeka
SS0105.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons.
SS0105.history: A Mundari agro-pastoralist county on both banks of the White Nile north of Juba. It was split off from Juba County in 2001, and its headquarters is Terekeka town.
SS0105.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported intercommunal violence by community-based militias around Juba and Terekeka counties in 2022. ACLED shows moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2018. Floods have displaced more people here than anything else. Terekeka is among the counties with the most flood displacement since 2020, and communal clashes have displaced thousands more. In 2018 more than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger, and a large minority still did in 2025.

SS0106.name: Yei
SS0106.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS0106.history: Yei River County is home to the Pojulu, Kakwa, Keliko, Makaraka, Mundu and others. Yei town, near Uganda and DR Congo, is a cross-border trade hub and hosts displaced people and Congolese refugees.
SS0106.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Yei as the centre of the 2018-19 conflict between government forces and the National Salvation Front (NAS). NAS abductions in Lasu, Otogo and Tore payams went on from 2022 to 2025. ACLED has recorded more political-violence events here than in almost any other county, and 2018 was the deadliest year. The displaced population has been fairly large, peaking in 2021. Hunger has been less severe than in most of the country, and the share of people in crisis has fallen since 2019.

SS0201.name: Budi
SS0201.livelihoods: Mostly crop farming, mainly sorghum, with a few livestock. There is one rainy season and not enough cereal, so people turn to forest and wild foods and sell bush products.
SS0201.history: Named after the Buya and Didinga agro-pastoralists who live there, Budi borders Uganda and Kenya. Its headquarters, Chukudum, hosted the first SPLM National Convention in 1994.
SS0201.conflict_impact: In 2024 UNMISS reported an attack on Didinga honey harvesters in Budi's mountains, an area contested with Karamojong communities from Uganda. ACLED records relatively high political violence for the county, much of it aimed at civilians, and deaths peaked in 2021. Fairly few people have been displaced. Hunger was severe in 2019, when most residents were in crisis-level food insecurity or worse, but it has eased a good deal since.

SS0202.name: Ikotos
SS0202.livelihoods: Mostly crop farming, mainly sorghum, with a few livestock. There is one rainy season and not enough cereal, so people turn to forest and wild foods and sell bush products. Also partly in the Equatorial maize and cassava zone.
SS0202.history: A highland county around Ikotos town. The Lango, Ketebo and other agro-pastoral groups grow sorghum and millet here, and dry-season cattle raiding has a long history, especially in the Kidepo valley.
SS0202.conflict_impact: In 2024 UNMISS documented incursions by armed Logir groups into Chokorol payam that killed and injured civilians. ACLED shows a moderate level of political violence, with 2022 the deadliest year. Communal clashes have displaced thousands of people since 2020. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, but food security is much better now.

SS0203.name: Kapoeta East
SS0203.livelihoods: Herding of cattle, goats and sheep with very little cropping in a semi-arid zone. Wild foods and market purchases, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0203.history: The Toposa pastoralists are the largest group, with a Jie minority in Jie payam and the Nyangatom near the Kenya-Ethiopia border. Payams include Narus, Natinga and Kauto.
SS0203.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported attacks on Toposa communities by armed Turkana from Kenya in 2023, and raids by armed Murle from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area in 2024-25. Political violence is moderate by ACLED's count, and deaths climbed to their highest in 2024. Communal violence has displaced thousands since 2020. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019. The share has fallen but is still large.

SS0204.name: Kapoeta North
SS0204.livelihoods: Herding of cattle, goats and sheep with very little cropping in a semi-arid zone. Wild foods and market purchases, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0204.history: A Toposa pastoralist county. Riwoto is its main settlement.
SS0204.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported armed Murle from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area reaching parts of Kapoeta North in 2024. ACLED data show moderate political violence, and 2022 was the deadliest year. Fewer people have been displaced than in most counties. Hunger peaked in 2019, when most residents were affected, and has eased since, but a large minority are still in crisis.

SS0205.name: Kapoeta South
SS0205.livelihoods: Herding of cattle, goats and sheep with very little cropping in a semi-arid zone. Wild foods and market purchases, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0205.history: A Toposa and Didinga county around Kapoeta town, the county headquarters. Kapoeta Mission Hospital serves a wide area, including returnees and displaced people.
SS0205.conflict_impact: ACLED has recorded relatively little political violence in Kapoeta South, though deaths rose to their highest in 2024. Displacement has been limited and peaked in 2019. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019. Conditions have improved, but a sizeable minority are still in crisis.

SS0206.name: Lafon
SS0206.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products. Also partly in the South-Eastern semi-arid pastoral zone.
SS0206.history: Also called Lopa or Lafon. The Lopit are the largest community, followed by the Pari, Tennet and Lotuko, and most people farm a single season.
SS0206.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported raids by armed Murle from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area on Pari and Toposa communities in Lafon between 2023 and 2025. ACLED records little political violence overall, with the most deaths in 2023. Displacement has kept growing and was highest in early 2025, and floods have displaced thousands. In 2023 more than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger, and close to half still were in 2025.

SS0207.name: Magwi
SS0207.livelihoods: Mostly crop farming, mainly sorghum, with a few livestock. There is one rainy season and not enough cereal, so people turn to forest and wild foods and sell bush products.
SS0207.history: An Acholi county on the Uganda border. Its towns include Magwi (the headquarters), Nimule, Pageri, Palotaka and Pajok, and the White Nile enters the country at Nimule.
SS0207.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported intercommunal violence involving Dinka Bor cattle keepers in and around Magwi in the first half of 2022. Political violence is moderate in ACLED's data, and 2022 was also the deadliest year. Displacement peaked that year too and was relatively high. Communal clashes alone have displaced tens of thousands since 2020. Hunger has been less severe than in most counties and has eased further since 2019.

SS0208.name: Torit
SS0208.livelihoods: Mostly crop farming, mainly sorghum, with a few livestock. There is one rainy season and not enough cereal, so people turn to forest and wild foods and sell bush products.
SS0208.history: Torit town, capital of Eastern Equatoria, is the county seat. The Lotuko (Otuho), Madi and Acholi live here, and the county was affected by the Second Sudanese Civil War and by the LRA.
SS0208.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported armed Murle from the Greater Pibor Administrative Area reaching parts of Torit County in 2023-24. ACLED counts a relatively high number of political-violence events, and deaths peaked in 2022. Internal displacement has been among the lowest in the country, though some people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. Food insecurity is lower than in much of South Sudan. About half of residents were in crisis in 2019, and fewer are now.

SS0301.name: Akobo
SS0301.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products.
SS0301.history: A Lou Nuer county on the Ethiopian border, with its headquarters at Akobo town. Herders move with their livestock to find water and pasture, and some residents have taken refuge in Ethiopia.
SS0301.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented repeated rounds of attacks and cattle raids between Lou Nuer and Murle communities that affected Akobo in 2020 and again from 2022 to 2024. ACLED records relatively high political violence, often aimed at civilians, and deaths peaked in 2023. Floods and armed conflict have each displaced thousands since 2020. Hunger has been severe. In 2022 a large majority of residents were in crisis-level food insecurity or worse, and more than half still were in 2025.

SS0302.name: Ayod
SS0302.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0302.history: Home to the Gawaar (Gaawar) Nuer, on the Sudd-edge floodplain of northern Jonglei.
SS0302.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported that the Gawaar Nuer 'White Army' militia from Ayod fought with the Kitgwang faction in Upper Nile between August and December 2022. By ACLED's count political violence is moderate, and deaths rose to their highest in 2025. Floods are a main cause of displacement: Ayod is among the counties where floods have driven the most people from home since 2020, and armed conflict has displaced thousands more. In 2022 a large majority of residents were in crisis-level hunger. Conditions have eased since, but nearly half are still in serious need.

SS0303.name: Bor South
SS0303.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products.
SS0303.history: A Dinka Bor county on the east bank of the White Nile. It contains Bor town, the capital of Jonglei State.
SS0303.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported armed Murle raids into Bor South in 2020 and 2023-24, and also reported Dinka Bor cattle keepers taking part in violence around Magwi in 2022. ACLED records relatively high political violence, with the most deaths in 2020. Bor South has one of the largest displaced populations in the country, which peaked in 2023, and communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands since 2020. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2018, but conditions are much better now.

SS0304.name: Canal/Pigi
SS0304.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products.
SS0304.history: A county in northwestern Jonglei along the White Nile, home to Padang Dinka (Paweny, Thoi, Rut, Luac), Gawaar and Lou Nuer, and Shilluk communities.
SS0304.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported that armed groups from Pigi joined the 2022 fighting in Upper Nile, and that violence spilling over from Upper Nile hit Pigi and neighbouring Fangak in 2025. ACLED records relatively few deaths overall, but 2025 had the most. The displaced population is one of the largest in the country and peaked in 2023, and floods have displaced thousands more. Hunger here is among the worst in South Sudan. A large majority of residents were in crisis-level food insecurity or worse in 2019, and most still were in 2025.

SS0305.name: Duk
SS0305.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0305.history: A mainly Dinka county (according to UNMISS) south of the Sudd. Duk Payuel is the birthplace of 'Lost Boy' John Dau.
SS0305.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented repeated armed Murle attacks on Duk in 2020 and 2023. In 2024 the county accounted for a disproportionate share of Jonglei's civilian victims of this violence. ACLED records relatively high political violence, often against civilians, and deaths peaked in 2024. Displacement reached its highest point in early 2025, and floods have displaced thousands. A large majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2018. The share has fallen, but a large minority are still in crisis.

SS0306.name: Fangak
SS0306.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile and the Sudd. People fish, grow sorghum and maize, keep cattle, goats and sheep, and gather water lilies and other wild foods. Floods return every few years. Also partly in the Eastern plains sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0306.history: Mostly Laak and Thiang Nuer, agro-pastoralists of the Sudd. The headquarters, Phom el Zeraf, is where the Bahr el Zeraf meets the White Nile.
SS0306.conflict_impact: OCHA named Fangak the most flood-affected county in South Sudan in 2021. Fighting reached New Fangak in 2022, and air strikes on Old Fangak in May 2025 killed civilians. Political violence is moderate overall in ACLED's data, with the most deaths in 2025. IOM displacement tracking shows that since 2020, floods and armed conflict have each displaced more people in Fangak than in any other county. Its displaced population was among the largest in the country in 2024, and many people fleeing the war in Sudan have also arrived. Hunger is among the worst in South Sudan. A large majority of residents were in crisis-level food insecurity or worse in 2022, and nearly as many still were in 2025.

SS0307.name: Nyirol
SS0307.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products.
SS0307.history: A Lou Nuer county (according to UNMISS) in northern Jonglei. Lankien is one of its main towns.
SS0307.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Murle raids on Nyirol in 2020 and 2023-24, and a 2022 attack in Fashoda by Lou Nuer youth from Lankien. ACLED records relatively high political violence, often aimed at civilians, and deaths peaked in 2024. Communal clashes and wider armed conflict have each displaced thousands since 2020, and the displaced population was largest in 2023. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, and more than half still were in 2025.

SS0308.name: Pibor
SS0308.livelihoods: Herding of cattle, goats and sheep with very little cropping in a semi-arid zone. Wild foods and market purchases, including grain from Kenya and Ethiopia, fill the food gap.
SS0308.history: Home of the Murle, Kachipo and Jie, and seat of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA), announced in 2020. The headquarters is Pibor town, and other areas include Gumuruk, Likuangole and Verteth.
SS0308.conflict_impact: According to UNMISS, Dinka and Nuer militias attacked Likuangole and Gumuruk in 2020, and Nuer militias launched a large attack on the Greater Pibor Administrative Area on 24 December 2022. In ACLED's data Pibor is one of the deadliest counties in South Sudan, and 2022 was its worst year. Communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands since 2020. Hunger is among the worst in the country. A large majority of residents were in crisis-level food insecurity or worse in 2022, and most still were in 2025.

SS0309.name: Pochalla

livelihood_zone.name: Maize Sorghum Fishing and Natural Resources

SS0309.livelihoods: Farming of maize and sorghum with two harvests a year, plus livestock, fishing and natural resources such as honey and shea from the Boma/Badingilo area.
SS0309.history: An Anyuak (Anuak) farming county on the Ethiopian border, part of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area. It hosts Anyuak refugees from Ethiopia.
SS0309.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported incursions by armed Murle into parts of Pochalla in 2024. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with the most deaths in 2023. Floods and armed conflict have each displaced thousands, and displacement peaked in 2024. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2023, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0310.name: Twic East
SS0310.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0310.history: A Twic (Twi) Dinka county with its headquarters at Panyagor. It was the Twi Dinka district in colonial times and is the birthplace of John Garang.
SS0310.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Murle raids into Twic East in 2020 and 2024. Political violence is moderate by ACLED's count, and deaths were highest in 2025. Floods have displaced thousands since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2024. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0311.name: Uror
SS0311.livelihoods: Rain-fed sorghum and cattle herding on the floodplains, with fishing, hunting and wild foods. The area grows too little cereal but has plenty of fish and livestock products.
SS0311.history: A Lou Nuer county in northern Jonglei, and home area of Gen. Simon Gatwech Dual, a former SPLA-IO chief of staff.
SS0311.conflict_impact: UNMISS documented Murle raids on Uror in 2020 and 2023, part of a longer cycle of violence between Lou Nuer and Murle communities. ACLED ranks Uror among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2020. Floods, communal clashes and wider armed conflict have together displaced tens of thousands since 2020. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and more than half still were in 2025.

SS0401.name: Awerial
SS0401.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0401.history: An Aliab Dinka county with its headquarters at Mingkaman on the White Nile. By January 2014 Mingkaman had taken in tens of thousands of people displaced from Bor South, Twic East and Duk, though the county saw little fighting itself in 2013-18.
SS0401.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that raiding between Aliab Dinka and Mundari communities near the Terekeka border increased in 2020-21, and that severe Nile flooding in mid-2020 displaced riverside settlements. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with the most deaths in 2020. Awerial has hosted one of the largest displaced populations in the country, peaking in 2019, because Mingkaman has sheltered people fleeing fighting in Jonglei since 2014. Floods have displaced tens of thousands more. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and the share has dropped a lot since.

SS0402.name: Cueibet
SS0402.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons.
SS0402.history: A Gok Dinka county with its headquarters at Cueibet town. It was relatively sheltered from the 1983-2005 and 2013-2018 wars, but fighting between Gok sections has affected it since the late 1990s.
SS0402.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that raiding between sections increased after the 2018 peace agreement (R-ARCSS), with cross-border violence involving Agar Dinka in 2021 and Tonj South in late 2022, before it eased from 2022. ACLED ranks Cueibet among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2021. Relatively few people have been displaced. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, but food security is much better now.

SS0403.name: Rumbek Centre

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0403.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0403.history: An Agar Dinka county containing Rumbek, the capital of Lakes State and the SPLM/A headquarters after 1997. The 2013-2018 fighting between the SPLA and SPLA-IO did not reach it directly.
SS0403.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that after 2018, clashes among Agar Dinka sections and with Gok Dinka became more lethal, and that a new state governor imposed coercive security measures from 2021. ACLED records relatively high political violence, with deaths peaking in 2021. Displacement within the county has been among the lowest in the country. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0404.name: Rumbek East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0404.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain. Also partly in the Ironstone Plateau agro-pastoral zone.
SS0404.history: An Agar Dinka county with its headquarters in Aduel payam. Feuds within and between sections, and cattle raiding from southern Unity State, have long affected it.
SS0404.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that fighting between the Gony and Thuyic sub-sections escalated in 2019-2021 despite a peace deal in November 2019, and that violence across the border with Yirol West also flared. ACLED records relatively high political violence, with the most deaths in 2021. Displacement has been fairly limited. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and that share has since fallen below half.

SS0405.name: Rumbek North

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0405.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0405.history: A Pakam (Agar) Dinka county where Lakes, Warrap and Unity meet. Disputes over water and grazing, and cattle raiding, are common.
SS0405.conflict_impact: Fighting between the Gak and Manuer sections killed dozens of people in November 2019. Clashes between Pakam and Luach-Jang communities on the Tonj East border caused heavy loss of life in February and April 2023 (CSRF, UN Security Council). ACLED ranks Rumbek North among the deadliest counties in the country, and 2023 was its worst year. Displacement was relatively high and peaked in late 2019. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2020, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0406.name: Wulu
SS0406.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons.
SS0406.history: Home to the Belle ('Jur Bel') and Bongo, who farm and fish. The county hosted the 2000 follow-up to the Wunlit peace conference.
SS0406.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that raids on cattle camps continued after 2018, including the killing of Gok Dinka cattle traders in December 2019, and that road security improved from 2022. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with the most deaths in 2021. Few people have been displaced. More than half of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2018, but food security has improved a lot since.

SS0407.name: Yirol East

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0407.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile and the Sudd. People fish, grow sorghum and maize, keep cattle, goats and sheep, and gather water lilies and other wild foods. Floods return every few years. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0407.history: A Ciec Dinka (Ador, Lou) and Atuot county in Greater Yirol, an SPLM/A stronghold in the second civil war. It includes the Nile port of Shambe.
SS0407.conflict_impact: Raiders from Panyijiar in Unity State are a recurring threat. In June 2025 UNMISS reported a deadly attack on a boat carrying Nuer civilians in Yirol East. ACLED data show moderate political violence, and 2025 was the deadliest year. Floods and communal clashes have displaced thousands since 2020. In 2018 a large majority of residents were in crisis-level hunger, and by 2025 about half were.

SS0408.name: Yirol West
SS0408.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons.
SS0408.history: An Atuot (Reel, Apak) county around Yirol town and Lake Yirol in Greater Yirol. Its payams include Aluakluak, Geer and Mapuordit.
SS0408.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that clashes between Agar Dinka and Atuot communities rose sharply in 2021 in Aluakluak and Gher payams, and that the Atuot community had a deadly internal clash the same year. ACLED records moderate political violence, with deaths peaking in 2021. Communal violence has displaced thousands, and displacement also peaked in 2021. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and the share has fallen considerably since.

SS0501.name: Aweil Centre

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0501.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum. Forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep add to it. The area used to produce a surplus. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0501.history: Home to Luo ('Jur Chol') and Dinka Malual communities, with its headquarters in Aroyo payam. It escaped most of the raiding of the second civil war and the 2013-2018 fighting, and took in displaced people from Wau and Raja.
SS0501.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that recent tensions concern land and water points, and disputes between Luo farmers and Fulani pastoralists, which peace conferences took up in 2021 and 2023. ACLED records very little political violence, among the lowest of any county. Floods have displaced thousands since 2020, and a substantial number of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived since 2023. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0502.name: Aweil East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0502.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0502.history: The most populous Dinka Malual (Abiem) county, with its headquarters at Mabil (Wanyjok area). Murahalin raids hit it hard in the 1983-2005 war, and several national leaders come from here.
SS0502.conflict_impact: CSRF describes Aweil East as less directly affected by the 2013-18 war, though SSPM/A rebels were active in 2016-18 and caused some displacement. Political violence is moderate in ACLED's data, with the most deaths in 2020. Floods drive most displacement, and Aweil East is among the most flood-affected counties since 2020. Since 2023 it has also been one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0503.name: Aweil North

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0503.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0503.history: A Dinka Malual (Giernyang) county with its headquarters at Gok Machar, on the disputed border with Sudan, including the '14-Mile Area'. Murahalin raids hit it badly in 1983-2005.
SS0503.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that Aweil North was directly affected early in the 2013-18 war. Since 2023 the state has taken in people fleeing the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan. ACLED has recorded very little political violence here since 2018. Floods cause most displacement, and Aweil North is among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020. It has also received a substantial number of arrivals from Sudan. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2020, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0504.name: Aweil South

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0504.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0504.history: A Dinka Malual (Paliet) and Luo ('Jur Chol') county with its headquarters in Nyocawany payam, away from the Sudan border. The 2013-2018 war had little direct effect here.
SS0504.conflict_impact: CSRF describes mostly low-level, local conflict since 2018, such as an April 2019 dispute among Paliet sub-sections over the Wathmuok boundary that a peace conference settled. ACLED records very little political violence, among the lowest of any county. Floods have displaced thousands since 2020. Hunger has got worse recently. Crisis-level food insecurity was highest in 2024, when most residents were affected, and more than half still were in 2025.

SS0505.name: Aweil West

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0505.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0505.history: A Dinka Malual and Luo ('Jur Chol') county with its headquarters at Nyamlel. Militia raids hit Nyamlel and Marial Bai hard during the 1983-2005 war.
SS0505.conflict_impact: CSRF reports isolated incidents between Dinka Malual and Rizeigat communities in 2020-21 and land disputes in 2022-24, far below the violence of the second civil war. ACLED records very little political violence. Even so, the displaced population has been relatively large, peaking in 2019. Floods have displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and a substantial number of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0601.name: Abiemnhom
SS0601.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0601.history: A Padang Dinka (Alor) county on the disputed Sudan border, part of the Ruweng Administrative Area (RAA) set up in 2020.
SS0601.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that road ambushes and tension between Bul Nuer and Alor Dinka communities have been the main problems since 2018, including a deadly cattle raid in 2022. By ACLED's count political violence is moderate, and 2025 was the deadliest year. Relatively few people have been displaced. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0602.name: Guit

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0602.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral, with more weight on cattle than on crops. Maize is the main staple, fishing and wild foods add to it, and the zone relies on grain imported from Sudan. Also partly in the Nile basin fishing and agro-pastoral zone.
SS0602.history: A Western Jikany Nuer county created in 2005. SPLA-IO held most of it in 2013-2018, despite government offensives in 2014, 2015 and 2018.
SS0602.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that police officers were killed chasing raiders from Mayom in May 2021, that clashes between Guit and Pariang communities turned deadly in February 2022, and that the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO fought in December 2023. ACLED records moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2018. Displacement has grown and was highest in early 2025, and floods have displaced thousands. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, and most still were in 2025.

SS0603.name: Koch

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0603.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral, with more weight on cattle than on crops. Maize is the main staple, fishing and wild foods add to it, and the zone relies on grain imported from Sudan.
SS0603.history: A Jagey (Jagei) Nuer county in central Unity. It was a frontline in past wars and is the site of the Thar Jath oil field.
SS0603.conflict_impact: Fighting around the Mirmir SPLA-IO cantonment site in February-April 2022 was part of the wave of violence in southern Unity in which UNMISS documented large-scale killings of civilians. ACLED data show moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2021. Floods have displaced tens of thousands since 2020. A large majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2018, and most still did in 2025.

SS0604.name: Leer

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0604.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile and the Sudd. People fish, grow sorghum and maize, keep cattle, goats and sheep, and gather water lilies and other wild foods. Floods return every few years. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0604.history: A Dok Nuer county. Leer town was an SPLA-IO stronghold and a target of government offensives, including in 2018.
SS0604.conflict_impact: UNMISS reports that between February and May 2022, attacks by government forces and allied militias centred on Leer killed and raped large numbers of civilians and displaced tens of thousands across southern Unity. ACLED records relatively high political violence, and deaths and displacement both peaked in 2022. Communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands since 2020. A large majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2018, and about half still did in 2025.

SS0605.name: Mayendit

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0605.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0605.history: A Haak Nuer county in southern Unity. It was an SPLA-IO stronghold and was hit by government offensives in 2014, 2015 and 2018.
SS0605.conflict_impact: Cattle raids from Tonj in 2019-20 and tension between government and opposition forces continued, and UNMISS implicated Mayendit-based militias in the 2022 attacks on Leer. ACLED records moderate political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022. Floods have displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and displacement was highest in early 2025. A large majority of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and the share has since fallen below half.

SS0606.name: Mayom

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0606.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral, with more weight on cattle than on crops. Maize is the main staple, fishing and wild foods add to it, and the zone relies on grain imported from Sudan.
SS0606.history: A Bul Nuer county with its headquarters at Mayom town. It is the home of influential commanders such as the late Paulino Matip.
SS0606.conflict_impact: Splits among local elites led to the SSPM/A rebellion. In July 2022 an attack on Mayom town killed several people, including the county commissioner (CSRF, OHCHR). ACLED ranks Mayom among the deadliest counties in the country, with many civilians targeted and the most deaths in 2019. Floods have displaced tens of thousands since 2020, displacement was highest in early 2025, and thousands of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0607.name: Panyijiar

secondary.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0607.livelihoods: Riverine livelihoods along the Nile and the Sudd. People fish, grow sorghum and maize, keep cattle, goats and sheep, and gather water lilies and other wild foods. Floods return every few years. Also partly in the Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle zone.
SS0607.history: A Nyuong Nuer county lying mostly in the Sudd wetlands, on the border with Lakes State. It was an opposition stronghold and was hit by government offensives in 2014-2015.
SS0607.conflict_impact: Cattle raiding with communities across the border in Lakes State (Rumbek and Yirol) recurred from 2021 to 2025, despite peace deals in 2018, 2022 and September 2024 (CSRF, UNMISS). Political violence is moderate in ACLED's data, and 2025 was the deadliest year. Floods cause most displacement, and Panyijiar is among the counties where flooding has displaced the most people since 2020. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0608.name: Pariang
SS0608.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0608.history: A Padang Dinka (Ruweng/Panaruu, Paweny) county and seat of the Ruweng Administrative Area created in 2020. It stayed loyal to the government in 2013-2018 and hosts Nuba Mountains refugees at Ajoung Thok, Pamir and Yida.
SS0608.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that local insecurity is concentrated in Wunkur payam, where the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO fought a deadly clash in July 2023. ACLED records moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2022. Since 2023 the county has received thousands of people fleeing the war in Sudan, on top of the refugees from Sudan's Nuba Mountains it has hosted for years. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0609.name: Rubkona

livelihood_zone.name: North-Western Nile basin cattle and maize

SS0609.livelihoods: Agro-pastoral, with more weight on cattle than on crops. Maize is the main staple, fishing and wild foods add to it, and the zone relies on grain imported from Sudan.
SS0609.history: A Leek Nuer county containing Bentiu, the Unity State capital, and Rubkona town, the centre of the Unity oil fields. Its large UNMISS PoC site became an IDP camp in 2021.
SS0609.conflict_impact: Severe floods in 2021-22 surrounded Bentiu, and the town's displacement camp depends on dykes to stay dry (MSF). In March 2022 a group of Misseriya herders was killed in a grazing dispute (UN Security Council). ACLED records moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2021. Rubkona hosts the largest displaced population of any county, which peaked in 2023, and is one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. Floods have displaced tens of thousands more. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and most still were in 2025.

SS0701.name: Baliet
SS0701.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0701.history: A Padang Dinka (Ngok Lual Yak) county in central Upper Nile, east of Malakal and crossed by the Sobat. There are land disputes with the Nuer to the south and the Shilluk along the Nile.
SS0701.conflict_impact: ACLED records moderate political violence in Baliet, much of it directed at civilians, and deaths rose to their highest in 2025. Communal clashes have displaced thousands since 2020, though overall displacement peaked in 2018. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, and more than half still were in 2025, a higher share than in most counties.

SS0702.name: Fashoda
SS0702.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0702.history: The Shilluk (Chollo) see Fashoda as the heart of their kingdom. It includes Kodok, the county seat, and Tonga. Territorial disputes between the Shilluk and Padang Dinka go back to the second civil war.
SS0702.conflict_impact: From August to December 2022, fighting between the Kitgwang faction with its allied White Army militia and Agwelek forces hit Tonga and Kodok, and tens of thousands of people sheltered at Kodok near the UNMISS base. ACLED records relatively high political violence, much of it against civilians, with deaths peaking in 2022. Communal violence has displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and a substantial number of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0703.name: Longochuk
SS0703.livelihoods: Livelihoods on the Sobat River floodplain, where maize growing, cattle and fishing are equally important. The zone imports cereal and is fairly isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0703.history: An Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gajaak) and Koma county near Ethiopia and Sudan's Blue Nile. It largely backed the opposition in 2013-2018, when SPLA offensives displaced civilians.
SS0703.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that defections after 2018 led to fighting between SPLA-IO and former SPLA-IO forces in February-March 2022, and to clashes between the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO in Mathiang in June 2023. Despite this, ACLED has no political-violence events located in the county itself. Armed conflict has still displaced more people here than in most counties since 2020. A large majority of residents faced crisis-level hunger in 2018, and most still did in 2025, one of the highest levels in the country.

SS0704.name: Luakpiny/Nasir
SS0704.livelihoods: Livelihoods on the Sobat River floodplain, where maize growing, cattle and fishing are equally important. The zone imports cereal and is fairly isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0704.history: An Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gaagwang, Gaajok) county on the Sobat River around the port town of Nasir, a centre of Anya-Nya 2 and later opposition activity.
SS0704.conflict_impact: UNMISS reports that fighting between the national army (SSPDF) and the White Army began in Nasir in February 2025, spread along the Sobat River and drove a nationwide rise in violence. ACLED records relatively high political violence, with deaths highest in 2025. Armed conflict has displaced thousands since 2020, and a substantial number of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and nearly as many still were in 2025, among the highest levels in the country.

SS0705.name: Maban
SS0705.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0705.history: A Mabanese (Tom, Dagu, Buni) and Burun county that includes Bunj. Its large refugee camps hold far more people than the host population.
SS0705.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that militia violence and attacks on aid compounds in Bunj in 2018 and 2019 fell off after the 2018 peace deal, and that floods in late 2019 cut off access. ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with the most deaths in 2021. Communal violence has displaced tens of thousands since 2020. Maban already hosted large refugee camps and has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0706.name: Maiwut
SS0706.livelihoods: Livelihoods on the Sobat River floodplain, where maize growing, cattle and fishing are equally important. The zone imports cereal and is fairly isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0706.history: An Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gajaak) and Koma county on the Ethiopian border. Pagak was the SPLA-IO headquarters during 2013-2018, and a 2017-18 offensive drove tens of thousands into Ethiopia.
SS0706.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that SPLA-IO defections after 2018, especially in August 2019, caused tension within the Gajaak community and fighting in December 2019 and January 2020. ACLED data show moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2018. Displacement within the county has been fairly limited and peaked in 2020. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and the share has fallen considerably since.

SS0707.name: Malakal
SS0707.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0707.history: Contains Malakal, capital of Upper Nile since 1914, which both the Shilluk and Padang Dinka claim. Control of the town changed hands between the SPLA and SPLA-IO in 2013-2018. It hosts the Malakal PoC site.
SS0707.conflict_impact: UNMISS reports that tens of thousands of people fled to the Malakal Protection of Civilians site during the 2022 fighting in Upper Nile, and that ethnic clashes broke out there and at Upper Nile University in 2023. ACLED records moderate political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022. Malakal has one of the largest displaced populations in the country, which peaked in 2024, and is one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. Hunger has got worse recently. Most residents were in crisis-level food insecurity in 2024, the worst year, and nearly as many still were in 2025.

SS0708.name: Manyo
SS0708.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0708.history: A Shilluk (Chollo) county in the far north of the White Nile's west bank. It has disputes over land, water and grazing with neighbouring Renk.
SS0708.conflict_impact: UNMISS reports that fighting between Shilluk forces and militias allied with Kitgwang spread into Manyo in November and December 2022 and displaced thousands. Political violence is moderate by ACLED's count, with the most deaths in 2021. Displacement was highest in early 2025, floods have displaced thousands, and a substantial number of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and more than half still were in 2025.

SS0709.name: Melut
SS0709.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0709.history: An Ageer Dinka county on the east bank of the White Nile, containing the Melut oil basin. Its location made it strategically important in both civil wars.
SS0709.conflict_impact: CSRF describes Melut as relatively stable since 2018, and it took in thousands of people displaced by the 2022 fighting in Upper Nile (UNMISS). ACLED records relatively little political violence, with the most deaths in 2022. Floods have displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and thousands of people fleeing the war in Sudan have arrived. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2023, and about half still were in 2025.

SS0710.name: Panyikang
SS0710.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0710.history: A Shilluk (Chollo) and Padang Dinka county along the White Nile south of Malakal, at the edge of the Shilluk Kingdom. It was heavily fought over in 2013-2018.
SS0710.conflict_impact: According to UNMISS, the August 2022 conflict in Upper Nile started with clashes between Agwelek and Kitgwang forces in Panyikang on 10 August. ACLED records moderate political violence, with deaths peaking in 2022. Floods and communal clashes have displaced tens of thousands since 2020. Hunger has been among the worst in the country. A large majority of residents were in crisis-level food insecurity in 2018, and most still were in 2025.

SS0711.name: Renk
SS0711.livelihoods: Semi-arid agro-pastoralism based on sorghum and livestock, with Nile fishing, labour migration and petty trade. Near the Nile there is mechanised farming. Elsewhere farming is for subsistence, and the zone grows too little cereal.
SS0711.history: An Abialang Dinka county at the northern tip of South Sudan, around Renk town. It was strategically placed and fought over in past civil wars, and seasonal movements of Falata herders have led to disputes.
SS0711.conflict_impact: Since April 2023 the Joda/Wunthow border crossing in Renk has been the main way into South Sudan for people fleeing the war in Sudan, and hundreds of thousands have crossed there (REACH, MSF). ACLED records relatively little political violence, with the most deaths in 2023. Renk is among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2024. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2025, the highest share recorded for the county.

SS0712.name: Ulang
SS0712.livelihoods: Livelihoods on the Sobat River floodplain, where maize growing, cattle and fishing are equally important. The zone imports cereal and is fairly isolated near the Ethiopian border.
SS0712.history: An Eastern Jikany Nuer (Gaajok) county on the Sobat River, bordering Ethiopia and Jonglei, where Lou and Jikany Nuer lands meet.
SS0712.conflict_impact: CSRF and UNMISS report fighting between Lou and Jikany Nuer near Doma in March 2019, deadly clashes within the Gaajok community in May 2021, and the effects of the 2025 hostilities between the national army (SSPDF) and the White Army. ACLED data show moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2025. Since 2020 armed conflict has displaced more people here than in almost any other county. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and most still were in 2025, among the highest levels in the country.

SS0801.name: Gogrial East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0801.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0801.history: A Rek Dinka (Apuk-Giir) agro-pastoral county with its headquarters at Liet-Nhom. The 2013-2018 fighting did not reach it directly, but it was a major recruiting ground for government forces.
SS0801.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that land and boundary disputes, tied to competition among local elites, and cross-border violence with Unity State in 2019 have driven insecurity since 2018. ACLED records moderate political violence, often aimed at civilians, and deaths peaked in 2021. Since 2020 communal violence has displaced more people here than in almost any other county, and floods have displaced tens of thousands more. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, but conditions have improved since.

SS0802.name: Gogrial West

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0802.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0802.history: A Rek Dinka (Aguok and Apuk) county containing Kuajok, the Warrap State capital, and Gogrial town, the county headquarters. It was a recruitment base for state forces in 2014 and 2018-19.
SS0802.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that disputes with Jur River communities over Nyinakook have led to violence on and off, and that competition among elites has shaped local conflict since 2018. ACLED records relatively little political violence, with the most deaths in 2023. Floods cause most displacement. Gogrial West is among the counties where floods have displaced the most people since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2021. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, but the share has fallen considerably.

SS0803.name: Tonj East

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0803.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0803.history: A Luac-Jang and Rek Dinka county with its headquarters at Romic. It has rich dry-season grazing land on the borders of Lakes and Unity states.
SS0803.conflict_impact: The UN Panel of Experts reported that a 2020 disarmament campaign around Romic ended in heavy loss of life. UNMISS found that armed groups from Tonj East and Tonj North caused the most civilian victims in Warrap in 2024. ACLED ranks Tonj East among the deadliest counties in South Sudan, with deaths peaking in 2024. Since 2020 communal violence has displaced more people here than in almost any other county, and floods have displaced tens of thousands more. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0804.name: Tonj North

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0804.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0804.history: A Rek Dinka county with its headquarters at Warrap town. Greater Tonj elites are prominent in national politics, and the 2013-2018 war had only limited direct effects here.
SS0804.conflict_impact: Violence between clans and sub-sections has surged since 2019, amid recruitment linked to the 2018 peace agreement (R-ARCSS). UNMISS found that armed groups from Tonj East and Tonj North caused most of Warrap's civilian victims in 2024. ACLED has recorded more deaths from political violence in Tonj North than in any other county since 2018, including the most civilian deaths, and the toll peaked in 2021. Communal violence has displaced more people here than anywhere else in the country since 2020, floods have displaced tens of thousands more, and the displaced population is among the largest. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, and the share has fallen considerably since.

SS0805.name: Tonj South
SS0805.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons.
SS0805.history: A Rek Dinka and Bongo county around Tonj town, the largest town between Rumbek and Wau. There was no direct civil-war fighting here in 2013-2018.
SS0805.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that disputes over grazing, boundaries and cattle raiding led to repeated clashes in 2020, and that 2021 brought both drought and floods. ACLED records relatively high political violence, with deaths peaking in 2020. Since 2020 floods have displaced more people here than in most counties, and communal violence has displaced tens of thousands more; displacement peaked in 2021. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2022, but conditions have improved considerably.

SS0806.name: Twic

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0806.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0806.history: A Twic Mayardit Dinka county on the edge of the Abyei Area, with its headquarters at Turalei. The 2013-2018 fighting did not reach it directly.
SS0806.conflict_impact: UNMISS reports that border fighting between Twic and Ngok Dinka communities since February 2022 made Warrap the state with the most civilian victims in 2023. There were also clashes with youth from Mayom in 2022. ACLED ranks Twic among the deadliest counties in the country, with deaths peaking in 2023. The displaced population is one of the largest in South Sudan. Floods and communal violence have each displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and flood displacement here is among the highest anywhere. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS0001.name: Abyei

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0001.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Most households own cattle, and since the zone grows too little cereal, people trade livestock for grain.
SS0001.history: The Abyei Administrative Area has been contested between Sudan and South Sudan since boundary decisions in 1905. Ngok Dinka live mainly in the south and Misseriya mainly in the north. The UN force UNISFA polices the area.
SS0001.conflict_impact: Clashes at Kolom killed dozens of people in January 2020. Border violence between Twic and Ngok Dinka communities began in February 2022 and escalated again in late 2023 (CSRF, UNMISS). ACLED ranks Abyei among the deadliest areas in the country, with many civilians targeted and the most deaths in 2023. Since 2020 communal violence has displaced more people here than in almost any other area, and floods have displaced tens of thousands. Abyei has also become one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2023.

SS0901.name: Jur River

livelihood_zone.name: Greater Bahr el Ghazal sorghum and cattle

SS0901.livelihoods: Farming of sorghum (the staple), maize and groundnuts alongside cattle, goats and sheep, plus fishing and wild foods. Also partly in the Ironstone Plateau agro-pastoral and Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum zones.
SS0901.history: Home to Balanda Bor, Luo ('Jur Chol') and Dinka Marial Bai communities, with its headquarters at Nyin Akok. The 2014 clash at the Mapel training centre happened here, but the 2013-18 war otherwise had little direct impact.
SS0901.conflict_impact: Tens of thousands of people fled communal clashes between February and June 2019, especially in Kuarjena and Rocrocdong payams (IOM displacement tracking, via CSRF), and disputes between Luo and Dinka Marial Bai communities continue (UNMISS). ACLED records moderate political violence, often against civilians, with deaths peaking in 2019. Communal violence and floods have each displaced tens of thousands since 2020. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2019, but food security has improved a lot since.

SS0902.name: Raja

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS0902.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum. Forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep add to it. The area used to produce a surplus.
SS0902.history: The largest county, bordering Sudan and the Central African Republic. Many 'Fertit' groups (Kresh, Balanda, Banda, Aja and others) live around Raja town, which SPLA-IO briefly overran in June 2016.
SS0902.conflict_impact: According to CSRF, forces of Paul Malong's South Sudan United Front/Army (SSUF/A) were defeated in Raja in August 2019. Since 2023 tension has grown around gold mining at Boro Medina, and the road north to South Darfur is still insecure. ACLED records relatively little political violence in Raja compared with other counties, with the most deaths in 2018. Displacement within the county has been modest and peaked in 2019, though floods have forced thousands from their homes, and since 2023 Raja has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. Hunger was severe in 2018, when most residents were in crisis-level food insecurity or worse. It has eased since, but a sizeable minority are still in crisis.

SS0903.name: Wau

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS0903.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum. Forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep add to it. The area used to produce a surplus.
SS0903.history: Contains Wau, capital of Western Bahr el Ghazal, with Balanda and other 'Fertit', Luo ('Jur Chol') and Dinka communities. Attacks in Wau town in June 2016 drove large numbers of people into the UN PoC site.
SS0903.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that fighting between government and opposition forces around Mboro and Baggari in 2018 eased in 2019, but SPLA-IO defections and splits keep the Baggari area insecure. ACLED records moderate political violence, with the most deaths in 2018. Wau has hosted one of the largest displaced populations in the country, peaking in 2019, and has become one of the main destinations for people fleeing the war in Sudan. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, but food security has improved a lot since.

SS1001.name: Ezo

secondary.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1001.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this. Also partly in the Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum zone.
SS1001.history: A Zande (Azande) county with its headquarters at Ezo town, on the borders of DR Congo and the Central African Republic. It has long been exposed to LRA attacks and cross-border armed groups.
SS1001.conflict_impact: Tens of thousands of people fled the 2021 violence in Tambura into Ezo, and UNMISS reported that hundreds of young people from Ezo were recruited and sent to Tambura in September 2021 (CSRF). ACLED records relatively little political violence within the county, with the most deaths in 2025. Communal and armed conflict have displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and displacement peaked in 2022. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, but food insecurity in Ezo is now among the lowest in the country.

SS1002.name: Ibba
SS1002.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS1002.history: An Azande, Baka and Mundu county with its headquarters at Ibba town. The LRA carried out abductions here from 2005-06.
SS1002.conflict_impact: Clashes between residents and Mbororo-Fulani herders increased from 2022, and a deadly attack in spring 2023 displaced thousands (UN Security Council, via CSRF). ACLED records very little political violence compared with other counties. Apart from that attack, displacement has been limited. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, but food insecurity is now among the lowest in the country.

SS1003.name: Maridi
SS1003.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS1003.history: A Baka, Mundu, Avukaya, Zande and Moro Kodo county with its headquarters at Maridi town. Land disputes go back to land given to SPLA soldiers in the 1990s.
SS1003.conflict_impact: CSRF reports persistent tension between farmers and pastoralists over crop damage and contested land, and clashes between SPLA-IO and government forces in 2016-17. ACLED has recorded relatively little political violence since 2018, with the most deaths in 2021. Few people have been displaced. Food insecurity has been among the lowest in the country throughout the period.

SS1004.name: Mundri East
SS1004.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this. Also partly in the Ironstone Plateau agro-pastoral zone.
SS1004.history: A Moru and Mundu county with its headquarters at Kediba, on the border between Western and Central Equatoria. Herds from Lakes and Central Equatoria come here in the dry season.
SS1004.conflict_impact: UNMISS reported that operations by the national army (SSPDF) against the National Salvation Front (NAS), and abuses by NAS, harmed civilians in Mundri East in 2024. ACLED records little political violence overall, but deaths rose to their highest in 2025. Since 2020 armed conflict has displaced more people here than in almost any other county, and communal clashes have displaced thousands more. About half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and food insecurity is now relatively low.

SS1005.name: Mundri West
SS1005.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS1005.history: A Moru, Belle and Mundu county with its headquarters at Mundri town. Since 2005, farmers and herders in greater Mundri have grown increasingly divided.
SS1005.conflict_impact: UNMISS attributed many of the abductions in the Mundri area in 2020 to the National Salvation Front (NAS). ACLED records relatively little political violence compared with other counties, with the most deaths in 2023. Displacement has been among the lowest in the country, though armed conflict and floods have each displaced thousands since 2020. More than half of residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and food insecurity is now relatively low.

SS1006.name: Mvolo
SS1006.livelihoods: An agro-pastoral zone where households grow sorghum, groundnuts and other crops and keep cattle, goats and sheep. Output is moderate, water runs very short in the dry season, and cattle raids come with the seasons.
SS1006.history: A Belle ('Jur Bel'), Bongo, Wira, Nyamusa and Moru county with its headquarters at Mvolo town, closely tied to Wulu in Lakes. It hosted the Mvolo peace conference.
SS1006.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that security improved after the 2018 peace agreement (R-ARCSS), but violence by groups that often went unidentified rose again in 2020. ACLED records relatively little political violence, with the most deaths in that year. Displacement has been among the lowest in the country, though floods and communal clashes have each displaced thousands since 2020. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and the share has fallen considerably since.

SS1007.name: Nagero

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1007.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum. Forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep add to it. The area used to produce a surplus.
SS1007.history: A remote Balanda, Bongo and Azande county with its headquarters at Nagero town. SPLA-IO briefly took Nagero in May 2018 before an SPLA counter-offensive.
SS1007.conflict_impact: Nagero took in thousands of people, mostly Balanda, displaced by the 2021 violence in Tambura, and CSRF found that displaced people made up most of those in need. ACLED records relatively little political violence within the county, with the most deaths in 2025. Communal violence has displaced tens of thousands since 2020, and displacement was highest in early 2025. Most residents were in crisis-level hunger in 2018, and a large minority still were in 2025.

SS1008.name: Nzara

secondary.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1008.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this. Also partly in the Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum zone.
SS1008.history: A Zande county with its headquarters at Nzara town, where the July 1955 Nzara demonstrations took place within the colonial Zande Scheme. Little of the 2013-2018 conflict spread here.
SS1008.conflict_impact: CSRF reports occasional low-level insecurity since 2018, such as a June 2019 incident involving the national army (SSPDF) at Mogoroko and killings in Sakure payam in September 2021. ACLED has no political-violence events located in the county for the period. Few people have been displaced. Food insecurity in Nzara has been the lowest of any county, and few residents are in crisis-level hunger today.

SS1009.name: Tambura

livelihood_zone.name: Western plains groundnuts sesame and sorghum

SS1009.livelihoods: Subsistence rain-fed farming of groundnuts, sesame and sorghum. Forest products, seasonal river fishing and sales of poultry, goats and sheep add to it. The area used to produce a surplus.
SS1009.history: An Azande and Balanda county on the border with the Central African Republic, with its headquarters at Tambura town. It was part of the former Tambura State.
SS1009.conflict_impact: Violence between Azande and Balanda communities from June 2021 displaced tens of thousands of people (CSRF), and renewed tension in June 2024 brought many cases of sexual violence (UNMISS). ACLED records relatively high political violence, often against civilians, with deaths peaking in 2021. The displaced population was one of the larger ones in the country and peaked in 2022, mostly because of communal violence. Hunger in 2022 was among the worst in the country, with a large majority of residents affected, but it has eased considerably since.

SS1010.name: Yambio
SS1010.livelihoods: Rain-fed farming in the Greenbelt, which has two rainy seasons and normally produces a surplus of maize, sorghum, groundnuts, cassava and beans. Small livestock, fishing, hunting, wild foods and cross-border trade add to this.
SS1010.history: A Zande county containing Yambio, capital of Western Equatoria and historic seat of the Azande Kingdom, restored with a coronation in February 2022. It hosts refugees from DR Congo and the Central African Republic.
SS1010.conflict_impact: CSRF reports that clashes declined after 2018, but in 2021 officials were targeted in attacks and the national army (SSPDF) and SPLA-IO confronted each other in Yambio town. ACLED records relatively little political violence, with the most deaths in 2025. Displacement peaked in 2018 and has been moderate. Food insecurity has been among the lowest in the country, and few residents are in crisis-level hunger today.
